 
OSW/DRPMUxS -1 
Direct Report Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM UxS) 
2027 Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) BAA 
Release 1 
Proposal Submission Instructions 
INTRODUCTION 
The Office of the Secretary of War (OSW) SBIR/STTR Program supports the rapid maturation of 
commercial and dual-use technology to meet operational needs across the Department. Under this release, 
the Direct Report Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM UxS), in partnership with the Office 
of the Assistant Secretary of War for Special Operations and Low Intensity Conflict (OASW(SO/LIC)), is 
the sponsoring organization for the Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Rapid Maturation effort. 
These instructions apply to the following topics in this release: 
• OSW27BZ01-NV001, Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Rapid Maturation. This topic accepts 
Phase I proposals only. 
• OSW27BZ01-DV002, Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Rapid Maturation. This topic accepts 
Direct to Phase II proposals only. 
 
Proposers must select the topic corresponding to the type of proposal they intend to submit. The Phase I 
Proposal Guidelines below apply to OSW27BZ01-NV001. The Direct to Phase II Proposal Guidelines 
apply to OSW27BZ01-DV002. 
Proposers responding to a topic in this solicitation must follow all general instructions provided in the 
Department of War (DoW) SBIR Program solicitation. DRPM UxS requirements in addition to or 
deviating from the DoW Program solicitation are provided in the instructions below. Where these 
instructions and the DoW SBIR Program BAA conflict, the DoW SBIR Program BAA governs. 
Proposers are encouraged to thoroughly review the DoW solicitation and register for the DSIP 
Listserv to remain apprised of important programmatic and contractual changes. 
• The full DoW solicitation is available on DSIP at 
https://www.dodsbirsttr.mil/submissions/solicitation-documents/active-solicitations. Be sure to 
select the tab for the appropriate solicitation cycle. 
• Register for the DSIP Listserv at: https://www.dodsbirsttr.mil/submissions/login. 
 
Specific questions pertaining to the administration of the DRPM UxS SBIR/STTR Program and these 
proposal preparation instructions shall be directed to: Lerani Wolk, lerani.v.wolk.civ@mail.mil. 
PHASE I PROPOSAL GUIDELINES 
The guidelines in this section apply to topic OSW27BZ01-NV001. The DoW SBIR/STTR Innovation 
Portal (DSIP) is the official portal for DoW SBIR/STTR proposal submission. Proposers are required to 
submit proposals via DSIP; proposals submitted by any other means will be disregarded. Detailed 
instructions regarding registration and proposal submission via DSIP are provided in the DoW 
solicitation. 
Proposal Coversheet (Volume 1) 
The proposal coversheet is prepared on DSIP and in accordance with the DoW solicitation. The 
technical abstract and the anticipated benefits and commercial applications discussion may be 
publicly released if the proposal is selected. Do not include proprietary, export-controlled, 
controlled unclassified, or classified information in any coversheet field intended for public 
release. 
 
 
OSW/DRPMUxS -2 
Technical Volume (Volume 2) 
The technical volume is not to exceed two (2) pages and must follow the formatting requirements 
provided in the DoW SBIR solicitation, except that the Technical Volume must be uploaded as 
one searchable Portable Document Format (PDF), must use consecutively numbered pages, and 
must include the proposing small business concern's name, topic number, and DSIP-assigned 
proposal number in the header of each page. Graphics, tables, charts, references, and attachments 
included in Volume 2 count toward the page limit. Any pages in the technical volume over two 
pages will not be considered in proposal evaluations. 
Content of the Technical Volume 
The proposing small business concern must prepare Volume 2 using the Phase I Technical 
Volume Template provided as a separate attachment to this topic. The template identifies the 
content required in each section and corresponds to the criteria in the Phase I Evaluation Rubric. 
Volume 2 must state where the proposed approach stands against each of the four operating 
preferences identified in the topic. 
Cost Volume (Volume 3) 
The Phase I amount must not exceed $300,000. There is no priced option under this topic. The 
maximum Phase I period of performance is six (6) months. 
Cost is not an evaluation criterion under this topic. The Government will review Volume 3 for 
completeness, allowability, reasonableness, compliance with the cost ceiling, and compliance 
with applicable percentage-of-work requirements. 
Please review the updated Percentage of Work (POW) calculation details included in the DoW 
solicitation. DRPM UxS will not accept any deviation to the POW requirements. 
Company Commercialization Report (CCR) (Volume 4) 
Completion of the CCR as Volume 4 of the proposal submission in DSIP is required. Please refer 
to the DoW solicitation for full details on this requirement. Information contained in the CCR will 
not be considered by DRPM UxS during proposal evaluations. 
Supporting Documents (Volume 5) 
Volume 5 is provided for proposing Small Business Concerns (SBCs) to submit additional 
documentation to support the Coversheet (Volume 1), Technical Volume (Volume 2), and the 
Cost Volume (Volume 3). Please refer to the DoW solicitation for more information. Supporting 
documents must not be used to evade the Technical Volume page limit. Evaluators will consider 
only those documents identified as evaluable in these instructions and the applicable rubric. 
Fraud, Waste and Abuse Training (Volume 6) 
Fraud, Waste and Abuse training material can be found in the Volume 6 section of the proposal 
submission module in DSIP and must be thoroughly reviewed once per year to proceed with 
proposal submission. 
Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to Foreign Countries (Volume 7) 
SBCs must complete the Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to Foreign 
Countries webform in Volume 7 of the DSIP proposal submission. Please be aware that the 
Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to Foreign Countries WILL NOT be accepted 
as a PDF Supporting Document in Volume 5 of the DSIP proposal submission. Do not upload 
any previous versions of this form to Volume 5. For additional details, please refer to the DoW 
Program BAA. 
 
OSW/DRPMUxS -3 
DIRECT TO PHASE II (D2P2) PROPOSAL GUIDELINES 
The guidelines in this section apply to topic OSW27BZ01-DV002. 
15 U.S.C. §638 (cc), allows DoW to make a SBIR Phase II award to a small business concern with 
respect to a project, without regard to whether the small business concern was provided an award under 
Phase I of the SBIR program with respect to such project. 
This topic requires that proposers provide documentation to demonstrate that the feasibility described in 
the Phase I portion of the topic has been met. Feasibility documentation cannot be based upon or 
logically extend from any prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work. Work submitted 
within the feasibility documentation must have been substantially performed by the proposer and/or the 
principal investigator (PI). If technology in the feasibility documentation is subject to intellectual property 
(IP), the proposer must either own the IP or must have obtained license rights to such technology prior to 
proposal submission, to enable it and its subcontractors to legally carry out the proposed work. 
If the proposer fails to demonstrate technical merit and feasibility equivalent to the Phase I level as 
described in the associated topic, the related Phase II proposal will not be evaluated. 
DRPM UxS deviation from the standard Direct to Phase II volume structure: under this topic, the 
Technical Volume is limited to five (5) pages in total and constitutes the entire body of the D2P2 
technical proposal. Phase I-equivalent feasibility documentation is submitted separately, as evidence in 
Volume 5, limited to five (5) pages, rather than as part of Volume 2. This structure is intentional and 
reflects the short-form submission model used for this topic. 
Complete D2P2 proposals must include the following: 
• Volume 1: Proposal Cover Sheet 
• Volume 2: Technical Volume (5 page Maximum, total) 
• Volume 3: Cost Volume 
• Volume 4: Company Commercialization Report 
• Volume 5: Supporting Documents, including Phase I-equivalent feasibility documentation (5 
page Maximum) 
• Volume 6: Fraud Waste and Abuse Certification 
• Volume 7: Disclosure of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to Foreign Countries 
 
Phase II proposals require a comprehensive, detailed submission of the proposed effort. Commercial and 
military potential of the technology under development is extremely important. Proposals emphasizing 
dual-use applications and commercial exploitation of resulting technologies are sought. 
Volume 1 - Cover Sheet 
The proposal cover sheet is prepared on DSIP. The cover sheet must include a brief technical abstract that 
describes the proposed R&D project and an anticipated benefits and potential commercial applications 
discussion. Each section shall be no more than 3,000 characters. Do not include proprietary or 
classified information in the proposal cover sheet. If your proposal is selected for negotiation and 
possible award, the technical abstract and anticipated benefits discussion may be publicly released online.  
DSIP will assign a proposal number once the cover sheet is saved. You may modify the cover sheet as 
needed until the topic closes. 
Volume 2 - Technical Volume (5 pages) 
The Direct to Phase II Technical Volume must not exceed five (5) pages in total, inclusive of all graphics, 
figures, tables, charts, citations, and attachments contained in Volume 2. This five-page limit covers the 
entire body of the proposal. Pages exceeding the established limit will not be evaluated. The formatting 
 
OSW/DRPMUxS -4 
requirements stated in the Phase I Technical Volume section above apply equally to Direct to Phase II 
proposals. 
The proposing SBC must prepare Volume 2 using the Direct to Phase II Technical Volume Template 
provided as a separate attachment to this topic. The template identifies the content required in each 
section and corresponds to the criteria in the Direct to Phase II Evaluation Rubric. Volume 2 must state 
where the proposed approach stands against each of the four operating preferences identified in the topic. 
Proposers are responsible for planning and budgeting for required test authority, range access, spectrum 
authorization, threat surrogates, equipment, facilities, and other resources necessary to execute the 
proposed effort. 
Volume 3 - Cost Volume 
Direct to Phase II proposals must not exceed a cost of $2,000,000 and a duration of twelve (12) months. 
A detailed, Phase II Cost Volume must be submitted online and in the proper format shown in the Cost 
Breakdown Guidance in the DoW SBIR Program BAA. Some items in the cost volume template may not 
apply to the proposed project. Provide enough information to allow evaluators to assess the proposer's 
plans to use the requested funds if the contract is awarded. 
Cost is not an evaluation criterion under this topic. The Government will review Volume 3 for 
completeness, allowability, reasonableness, compliance with the cost ceiling, and compliance with 
applicable percentage-of-work requirements. DRPM UxS will not accept any deviation to the POW 
requirements. 
Volume 4 - Company Commercialization Report (CCR)  (Required) 
Completion of the CCR as Volume 4 of the proposal submission in DSIP is required. Please refer to the 
DoW SBIR Program BAA for full details on this requirement. The information contained in the CCR will 
not be considered during proposal evaluations. 
Volume 5 - Supporting Documents 
Volume 5 must include all documents and certifications required by the DoW SBIR Program BAA and 
these Component-Specific Proposal Submission Instructions. 
Phase I-equivalent feasibility documentation is required in Volume 5 and must not exceed five (5) 
pages. Feasibility documentation is supporting evidence and does not count toward the five-page 
Technical Volume limit. The documentation must demonstrate that: 
• The proposed technology has achieved the scientific and technical merit and feasibility described 
in the Phase I portion of this topic; 
• The documented work was substantially performed by the proposing SBC and/or the proposed PI; 
• The feasibility work was not based solely on, and does not logically extend from, prior or 
ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work; 
• The proposing SBC owns, or holds sufficient license rights to, any intellectual property necessary 
for the concern and its subcontractors to perform the proposed effort; and 
• The prior work supports the proposed technical approach, performance objectives, and transition 
or commercialization potential. 
 
Acceptable feasibility evidence may include test data, analyses, technical reports, prototype descriptions, 
modeling and simulation results, laboratory or field-test results, relevant internal research and 
development results, and other objective evidence of feasibility. A system design alone is not sufficient. A 
self-declared technology readiness level unsupported by a documented test is not sufficient. 
 
OSW/DRPMUxS -5 
Volume 5 may also include data-rights assertions, subcontractor or consultant letters of commitment, 
documentation supporting proposed costs, prior/current/pending support information, and foreign-citizen 
information, each as applicable. Supporting documents must not be used to evade the Technical Volume 
page limit. 
Volume 6 - Fraud Waste and Abuse Certification (Required) 
Fraud, Waste and Abuse training material can be found in the Volume 6 section of the proposal 
submission module in DSIP and must be thoroughly reviewed once per year to proceed with proposal 
submission. 
Volume 7 - Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to Foreign Countries (Required) 
Small business concerns must complete the Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to 
Foreign Countries webform in Volume 7 of the DSIP proposal submission. Please be aware that the 
Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to Foreign Countries WILL NOT be accepted as a 
PDF Supporting Document in Volume 5 of the DSIP proposal submission. Do not upload any previous 
versions of this form to Volume 5. For additional details, please refer to the DoW SBIR Program BAA. 
PHASE II PROPOSAL GUIDELINES 
Phase II proposals under OSW27BZ01-NV001 may only be submitted by Phase I awardees under that 
topic. A Phase I award does not guarantee a Phase II award. Subject to successful completion of Phase I, 
demonstrated technical progress, continued Government need, availability of funds, and all applicable 
statutory, regulatory, and DoW SBIR Program BAA requirements, a Phase I awardee may be eligible for 
a subsequent Phase II award without further competition. 
The Government may request a Phase II proposal from an eligible Phase I awardee during the Phase I 
period of performance or after Phase I completion. Any such request will provide the applicable proposal 
due date, technical requirements, cost and period-of-performance limits, evaluation criteria, and 
submission instructions. 
The anticipated Phase II objective is to mature the selected capability to a functional system, software 
package, or physical prototype suitable for test and evaluation in a militarily relevant or simulated field 
environment, with a target of Technology Readiness Level 6. The anticipated Phase II period of 
performance is twelve (12) months. Proposers shall not assume that a Phase I award, or a request for a 
Phase II proposal, constitutes a commitment of future funding. 
DISCRETIONARY TECHNICAL AND BUSINESS ASSISTANCE (TABA) 
The OSW SBIR/STTR Program will consider TABA requests in accordance with 15 U.S.C. § 638(q). 
Phase I awardees may request up to $6,500 in TABA funding; Phase II awardees may request up to 
$50,000 per Phase II project. TABA funding is in addition to the Phase I and Phase II cost ceilings and is 
not subject to profit/fee. Refer to the DoW Program BAA for detailed information about TABA funding, 
allowable services and requirements. 
All requests for TABA must be completed using the SBIR/STTR TABA Request Form found here. The 
completed form must be included in Volume 5 of the proposal submission in DSIP. OSW will not accept 
requests for TABA that do not utilize the SBIR/STTR TABA Request Form or as a submission document 
included in Volume 5. 
EVALUATION AND SELECTION 
All proposals will be evaluated in accordance with the evaluation criteria listed in the DoW solicitation. 
In addition, proposals under these topics will be evaluated using the criteria and rating approach in the 
separate evaluation rubric applicable to the proposal type:  
 
OSW/DRPMUxS -6 
Phase I Evaluation Rubric for OSW27BZ01-NV001  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
OSW/DRPMUxS -7 
Direct to Phase II Evaluation Rubric for OSW27BZ01-DV002 
 
 
 
 

 
OSW/DRPMUxS -8 
Direct to Phase II proposals will first undergo a feasibility determination using the Volume 5 feasibility 
documentation. Only proposals that establish Phase I-equivalent feasibility will proceed to evaluation of 
the technical proposal. If the Government determines that the proposer has not established feasibility, the 
proposal will not receive further evaluation. The Government will evaluate only the material permitted by 
these instructions and the applicable rubric. 
All awards are subject to the availability of funds. The Government reserves the right to make one or 
more awards, or no award, under either topic, and to limit the number of awards based on availability of 
funds. The Government is not obligated to make an award. Submission of a proposal does not authorize 
the proposer to begin work or incur costs on behalf of the Government. 
DRPMUxS uses support contractor personnel in the administration of these topics.  Support contractor 
personnel with access to proposal information are subject to non-disclosure obligations and may not 
participate in source selection decisions. 
Proposing firms will be notified of selection or non-selection status within 90 days of the closing date of 
the topic. Notification will be provided through DSIP to the Corporate Official identified in the proposal, 
with a copy to the Principal Investigator. 
Refer to the DoW solicitation for procedures to protest the Announcement. 
AWARD INFORMATION 
Direct Report Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM UxS) intends to execute prototype other 
transaction agreement awards as a result of this solicitation in accordance with 10 U.S.C. 4022.  
The projected Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) level at the time of award for these 
topics is Level 2 (Self). A firm without a current self-assessment posted in Supplier Performance Risk 
System (SPRS) is strongly encouraged to begin that process now. This must be completed by time of 
award. 
These topics are International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) restricted. The restriction paragraph 
published with each topic applies, including disclosure of any proposed use of foreign nationals. 
SBIR data rights attach to technical data and computer software developed under an award. Proposers 
shall mark proprietary material in accordance with the DoW SBIR Program BAA and shall assert any 
restricted or limited rights in the proposal rather than after award. 
ADDITIONAL INFORMATION 
Proposers are responsible for obtaining and accounting for the test authorities, range access, spectrum 
authorization, threat surrogates, equipment, facilities, and other resources necessary to execute the 
proposed effort. These requirements must be reflected in the proposed schedule and cost. 
Authority to mitigate or defeat unmanned aircraft in the United States is limited by statute to covered 
Federal entities. Proposers shall not assume that an award under either topic provides authority to mitigate 
or defeat unmanned aircraft, or guarantees access to Government ranges, spectrum, threat surrogates, test 
resources, or facilities. Where practicable, the Government may assist awardees in arranging range 
access, threat surrogates, or spectrum authorization. No such Government support is committed or 
guaranteed by this announcement. 
 
 
OSW/DRPMUxS -9 
The Government may host a capability showcase approximately six months after award. Attendance is by 
invitation and is based on end-user interest in the capability. It is not required of every performer. 
Performers shall provide operational evidence supporting a follow-on funding decision whether or not 
they are invited. 
 
  
 
OSW/DRPMUxS -10 
DRPMUxS SBIR DOW 2027 BAA 
Topic Index 
Release 1 
 
 
OSW27BZ01-NV001  Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Rapid Maturation 
 
OSW27BZ01-DV002  Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Rapid Maturation  
 
OSW/DRPMUxS -11 
OSW27BZ01-NV001 TITLE: Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Rapid Maturation 
 
OUSW (R&E) CRITICAL TECHNOLOGY AREA(S): Applied Artificial Intelligence 
 
COMPONENT TECHNOLOGY PRIORITY AREA(S): Trusted AI and Autonomy; Integrated Sensing 
and Cyber; Integrated Network Systems-of-Systems; Advanced Infrastructure & Advanced 
Manufacturing 
 
PROJECTED CMMC LEVEL REQUIREMENT: Level 2 (Self) 
 
The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 
22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, 
including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR 
Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items. Offerors must disclose any proposed use of foreign 
nationals (FNs), their country(ies) of origin, the type of visa or work permit possessed, and the statement 
of work (SOW) tasks intended for accomplishment by the FN(s) in accordance with the Announcement. 
Offerors are advised foreign nationals proposed to perform on this topic may be restricted due to the 
technical data under US Export Control Laws.  
 
OBJECTIVE: Mature commercial and dual-use technologies that detect, track, identify, or defeat small 
low-flying drones (Group 1 and Group 2 unmanned aerial systems) in hostile or contested areas. 
 
DESCRIPTION: Inexpensive, highly maneuverable, commercially available unmanned aerial systems 
(UAS) threaten tactical forces, critical infrastructure, and installations. Current defenses are limited by 
cost, by the operator attention they require, and by their vulnerability to countermeasures. A capability 
gap against Group 1 and Group 2 UAS remains. 
 
This topic seeks mature or maturing technology at any point in the counter-UAS kill chain. The three 
areas below are where capability is most needed. They are examples. A proposal may address one area, 
more than one, or a gap not listed here. 
 
Detection and Tracking. Detect and hold track on highly agile targets in cluttered low-altitude airspace. 
The proposer selects the sensing modality. Approaches that hold track when the target is not emitting are 
preferred. Solutions that require permanent site infrastructure or mains power, including fixed perimeter 
sensor installations, are out of scope for this area. The system must move with the force. 
 
Identification and Decision Support. Classify and identify unauthorized platforms and support an 
engagement decision. Processing must run on tactical computing hardware carried or emplaced with the 
force. Proposals should describe a pathway to interoperate with existing command and control. 
Conformance to a named standard is not required at this stage and will not be scored. 
 
Mitigation and Defeat. Kinetic, non-kinetic, or cyber approaches that defeat hostile UAS in remote 
tactical theaters and in densely populated areas. Proposals must address collateral effects. 
Operating preferences. The operating environment is denied, contested, and unattended. The four 
conditions below are preferences, not eligibility requirements.  
 
Every proposal must state where it stands against each one. 
(a) The system does not require the target to emit radio frequency (RF) energy. Passive RF may be part of 
a solution; the preference is that track holds when the target is silent. 
(b) The system does not radiate. The Government favors kinetic and cyber defeat over approaches that 
require the friendly system to emit. Jamming, active illumination, and transmission into a target's control 
 
OSW/DRPMUxS -12 
or navigation link are in scope. A proposal that uses any of them must say so and describe the operational 
effect. 
(c) The system does not require cloud services or reachback. Training and analytics may occur off-
platform. The processing that produces the operational output should run on the platform, and the system 
should continue to function with all external network interfaces disabled. 
(d) The system does not require a dedicated operator, meaning no person whose only task is attending it. 
Human judgment over the use of force is expected and is not addressed by this preference. 
 
Out of scope: work requiring classified access or a facility clearance at the time of award, and approaches 
that depend on cooperative identification, including Remote ID broadcast. 
 
PHASE I: Phase I shall determine the technical, scientific, and commercial feasibility of the proposed 
approach. Work may include developing a concept architecture, modeling critical software components, 
or bench testing key hardware elements. Phase I deliverables are a feasibility study, a technical report, 
and an initial system design package showing the path to a prototype. 
 
The technical report shall state the conditions, dates, and target or threat surrogate used in any testing 
performed, and the measured result. It shall also state where the approach stands against each of the four 
operating preferences. 
 
As required by the DoW solicitation, the feasibility documented may not rest solely upon, or logically 
extend from, prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work; the proposing firm and/or the 
principal investigator must have substantially performed the work relied upon; and the firm must 
demonstrate ownership or licensure of the associated intellectual property prior to proposal submission. 
 
PHASE II: Phase II follow-on depends on the availability of future-year funds and will be considered 
among the Phase I awardees under this topic. 
 
Phase II is a major research and development effort. Performers refine the Phase I concept into an 
operational prototype that demonstrates real-world functionality. The primary deliverable is a functional 
system, software package, or physical prototype ready for test and evaluation in a militarily relevant or 
simulated field environment. The technology shall reach TRL 6 by the end of Phase II. 
 
The period of performance is twelve months rather than the twenty-four the announcement allows. The 
intent is to move a demonstrated capability to a transition decision within one year. Proposals should be 
scoped to that schedule. 
 
The Government may host a showcase about six months after award. Attendance is by invitation and is 
based on end user interest in the capability. It is not required of every performer. Performers shall provide 
operational evidence supporting a follow-on funding decision whether or not they are invited. 
 
PHASE III DUAL USE APPLICATIONS: Commercial applications are those in which the equipment 
deploys with a team rather than being installed at a site: temporary airspace security for outdoor events, 
venues, and construction or energy sites; convoy, executive, and site-survey protection; wildfire, disaster, 
and critical infrastructure response; and mobile detection kits for law enforcement and allied partners. 
Detection, tracking, and identification technologies have a direct commercial market in these roles. 
Authority to mitigate or defeat unmanned aircraft in the United States is limited by statute to covered 
federal entities. A defeat-focused proposal is not expected to show a near-term domestic commercial 
market for that function. 
 
 
OSW/DRPMUxS -13 
Military applications include integration into point-defense systems for tactical units, forward operating 
bases, and naval vessel protection platforms, which may be funded via non-SBIR/STTR acquisition 
budgets.

artificial intelligence; multi-sensor fusion; denied environment

PHASE I: This topic solicits Direct-to-Phase-II (DP2) proposals only. Direct to Phase II proposers shall 
submit documentation showing that Phase I-equivalent feasibility has already been achieved outside the 
SBIR/STTR program. Adequate documentation is a written record of at least one test of the proposed 
approach stating the conditions under which the test was conducted, the dates, the target, threat, or 
surrogate used, the measured result, and how it was measured.Test data, technical reports, and third-party 
evaluation metrics are acceptable. A system design alone is not sufficient. A self-declared technology 
readiness level unsupported by a documented test is not sufficient. 
 
As required by the DoW solicitation, the feasibility documented may not rest solely upon, or logically 
extend from, prior or ongoing federally funded SBIR or STTR work; the proposing firm and/or the 
principal investigator must have substantially performed the work relied upon; and the firm must 
demonstrate ownership or licensure of the associated intellectual property prior to proposal submission. 
 
PHASE II: Phase II is a major research and development effort. Performers refine the Phase I concept into 
an operational prototype that demonstrates real-world functionality. The primary deliverable is a 
functional system, software package, or physical prototype ready for test and evaluation in a militarily 
relevant or simulated field environment. The technology shall reach TRL 6 by the end of Phase II. 
The period of performance is twelve months rather than the twenty-four the announcement allows. The 
intent is to move a demonstrated capability to a transition decision within one year. Proposals should be 
scoped to that schedule. 
 
The Government may host a showcase about six months after award. Attendance is by invitation and is 
based on end user interest in the capability. It is not required of every performer. Performers shall provide 
operational evidence supporting a follow-on funding decision whether or not they are invited. 
 
PHASE III DUAL USE APPLICATIONS: Commercial applications are those in which the equipment 
deploys with a team rather than being installed at a site: temporary airspace security for outdoor events, 
venues, and construction or energy sites; convoy, executive, and site-survey protection; wildfire, disaster, 
and critical infrastructure response; and mobile detection kits for law enforcement and allied partners. 
Detection, tracking, and identification technologies have a direct commercial market in these roles. 
Authority to mitigate or defeat unmanned aircraft in the United States is limited by statute to covered 
federal entities. A defeat-focused proposal is not expected to show a near-term domestic commercial 
market for that function. 
 
Military applications include integration into point-defense systems for tactical units, forward operating 
bases, and naval vessel protection platforms, which may be funded via non-SBIR/STTR acquisition 
budgets.
